title: Unburnable fire; God the overseer; houses without fear
english: “And may an arrow pass right through his body” (Job 20:25). These fiery arrows wound him.

“A fire that no one kindled will devour him” (Job 20:26). We are learning a mystery about the punishment that is laid up, so that we may guard against suffering it. He said that an unkindled fire will devour the ungodly man. This material fire that we have is not an unkindled fire, for it is seen. But that fire which comes upon sinners is invisible, and it burns them within. It is a fire of the mind, and it punishes. If you want to take an image of that fire, think, I ask you, of someone with a raging fever, burning as if with fire. You will not find the fire in him by looking; yet it lies beneath and burns up his inward parts. In the same way a person who is feverish from his sins is burned up.

“And may a newcomer ruin his house” (Job 20:26). The one who made war on that people was a newcomer and not a proselyte. He ruined his house, pulling down what was held to be a sanctuary and the city they called holy.

“And may heaven uncover his lawless deeds” (Job 20:27). That is: he will suffer terrible things both from God and from heaven. He said this because Job, after saying that he had been struck by God, also recalled that he had been wronged by men. So he argues that everything was brought upon him through sin. “And may the earth rise up against him” (Job 20:27). The earth itself rises up against that people.

“And a possession of goods is his from the Overseer” (Job 20:29). [Learn] who is named overseer here: God is called Overseer, and the overseers of the Church, the good and noble among them, strive in every way to bear his image. And just as the man who has copied a royal image is honoured for copying it well, and honoured too for having adorned it, so blessed is the overseer who has understood the true Overseer, who is zealous to be like him and becomes as God among men; or who has as his overseer the One who makes him truly an overseer in Christ Jesus. To him be the glory and the power for ever and ever. Amen.

“Look at me and be amazed” (Job 21:5). You claim to be wise and to know why I suffer these things, on the ground that God does not sleep over the sins of men. And you have dared to say that I am a sinner and have come to this justly.
“And they have grown old in wealth” (Job 21:7). They are not newly rich; they have spent many years being rich and always adding to their wealth.

“Their seed is according to the soul” (Job 21:8). The righteous man's seed is according to the spirit: for he sows to the spirit, and “of the spirit reaps eternal life” (Galatians 6:8). But with people of this kind, since “the man of soul does not receive the things of the Spirit, for they are foolishness to him” (1 Corinthians 2:14), the seed is not according to the spirit but according to the soul, the lesser part.

“And their children are before their eyes” (Job 21:8). Everything they do, they do “to be seen by men” (Matthew 23:5). For each person's works are his children. The children of those who hold other doctrines are not in the heart, in good thoughts, but before the eyes, to be seen by men.

“Their houses prosper” (Job 21:9). When you go into an assembly of heretics and see a crowd gathered there, see how their houses prosper. “And there is no fear anywhere” (Job 21:9). They are without fear. They do not fear God; they despise the Godhead. Saying such things about God, they are not afraid, though it is about God that they are speaking. “And there is no scourge from the Lord upon them” (Job 21:9).

From the same: If you see a man saying such things against God who is healthy in body, who sees, who keeps his senses whole, and who at times even seems to do well in the affairs of this world, see how in him, ungodly as he is, the words have been fulfilled: “And there is no scourge from the Lord upon them.”
“Their cow did not cast her calf” (Job 21:10).

From the same: The ox is a farming animal and works together with men at farming. They too farm. But what they farm is Sodom and Gomorrah; they farm Egypt. “Their cow did not cast her calf”: rather, she too brought forth and bore young, so that their wicked land might be farmed.

“And their pregnant one came safely through, and did not miscarry” (Job 21:10). Whatever they conceive, they also carry to term; they do not conceive from the fear of God but from wickedness. “Behold, he travailed with injustice, conceived trouble, and gave birth to lawlessness” (Psalm 7:14).

“And they remain like everlasting sheep” (Job 21:11). What is the meaning of “they will remain like everlasting sheep”? These are the ones of whom Christ says: “My sheep hear my voice, and I give them eternal life” (John 10:27-28), and so on. These are the everlasting sheep. title: Mimic flock; psalms of Valentinus; God teaches understanding
english: … flock of Christ, appointing for themselves bishops, presbyters, deacons, teachers, a laity and catechumens, they imitate the everlasting sheep and so fulfil the words: “They remain like everlasting sheep” (Job 21:11). But they are not everlasting sheep; they only remain like everlasting sheep.

“And their children make sport” (Job 21:11). “Taking up psaltery and harp” (Job 21:12). Our people take up psaltery and harp to sing hymns to God and give him glory. But the children of those men, senseless as they are within themselves, make sport as they take up psaltery and harp. Whenever they take up the words of the Old Testament, they make sport of them and laugh at the oracles of the Law and the Prophets. They take up the instruments that are in tune, the psaltery of the Law and the harp of prophecy, and make sport with them.

“And they rejoice at the sound of a psalm” (Job 21:12). They too recite psalms, the psalms of Valentinus, and recite odes, the odes of Basilides, and they utter things of that kind, rejoicing at the sound of a psalm.

“And in the rest of Hades they fell asleep” (Job 21:13). In rest, yes, but not the rest of heaven: it was in the rest of Hades that they fell asleep. But we pray to fall asleep not in the rest of Hades but in the rest of God, in the holy heavens, with Christ reigning over us. To him be the glory and the power for ever and ever. Amen.

“Is it not the Lord who teaches understanding and knowledge?” (Job 22:2). What the Holy Spirit arranges must be counted worthy of being written down. That is why it is written: so that the reader may profit from what he reads. So if the words of the three who came to Job had not been useful, so that the reader could take something from what they said to Job, providence would not have had the words of the three written into the book of Job as well. One may, then, profit from his words by looking closely at the doctrines, and see that what is blameworthy in the words concerns one thing only: they blame Job, thinking that he suffers because of the sins he has committed, and they do not see that there are many other causes of what happens to people. Such are the things that are reckoned good or hard, or whatever name one cares to give them.

And a little later: “Is it not the Lord who teaches understanding and knowledge?” The doctrine is sound: a human being cannot be a true teacher of virtue. For it is also written in the Psalms that the one who teaches man knowledge is no other than God (Psalm 94:10). And the Prophet says, “Teach me your just decrees” (Psalm 119:12), because he knows that God is the true and perfect teacher. God teaches by shining into the soul of the one who learns from him and by lighting up his mind with the light, his true Word. So righteous men too teach us, when they have received the grace of teaching.

“And he will enter into judgement with you” (Job 22:4). God, taking account of the one he cares for, reproves him. “And he will enter into judgement with you.” We have often said, whenever this doctrine came up in other words, that God loves mankind so much that, even as he judges us kindly, he allows us to speak to him about whatever we wish, as though he were on trial with us. So I used the words of Isaiah: “Come, and let us reason together, says the Lord” (Isaiah 1:18). For “let us reason together” means something like this: If you have any charge to bring against me and my providence, as though I had neglected you, as though I had not done what was needed, speak. And I will say whatever I have to say, and I will persuade you, condemning you as one who deserves to be condemned.

“Is not your wickedness great?” (Job 22:5). With good reason, I say, you have not simply been unjust; for he suffers things such as none of them has fallen into, things as great as yours. It is likely that these things have come upon you because your faults are past counting.

From the same: He did not name sin first and then wickedness. Rather, he looked at wickedness as the bad state of the soul, and after that at the sins committed from that bad state, which he said are sins past counting.

“And your sins are past counting” (Job 22:5). Eliphaz supposes this about Job. He knew that he was rich, and he says: You took pledges from your brothers as though they owed you, when they did not. For that is what “you took pledges for nothing” means. “You took pledges from your brothers for nothing” (Job 22:6).

From the same: Again he presses on to another sin of his. Is it ever possible to take clothing? Not from a naked man, but from a rich man who has many garments laid away. Three … then, the one of the many …

title: Naked cloak and empty widows; light turned dark; eternal path
english: … took clothing there: [not] from a naked man, but from a rich man. If, however, a man has a single tunic, and I strip that tunic off him on the pretext of claiming what is mine, without pity for the man left naked, then I have taken away the clothing of the naked. Many such things happen among us, whenever we lend money, whenever we go after our debtors. Often our debtor is poor beyond measure and cannot pay us back; and we shut up our hearts and become pitiless and cruel. We do not see that he is feeding a wife and children and can barely feed himself on the few small coins he scrapes together. We demand payment bitterly, and sometimes we do so while we ourselves have more than enough. This, then, is what he says in charging Job, that he took away the clothing of the naked.
“You did not even give water to the thirsty to drink, but you robbed the hungry of a morsel” (Job 22:7).

On the same words: So not only doing wrong but also failing to do good makes a person answerable. All these are charges, and truly blameworthy things. But they were not true of Job, and they were not rightly said about him.

From the same: Such things happen when debts are bitterly demanded. Sometimes a man has a single morsel and nothing more; even though he does not have a whole loaf, we take it from him, saying: But you owe.

“And you sent widows away empty” (Job 22:9). Let us take care that, if a widow comes into our house, we never send her away empty. Let each of us, as far as he is able, fill the widow's lap with what he has. “And you ill-treated orphans” (Job 22:9).

From the same: No one ought to be ill-treated, but orphans above all must be spared. For God commanded us to fight on behalf of helpless souls. More than other people, the poor, widows and orphans need help.
“Therefore snares have surrounded you” (Job 22:10). He calls snares the things that have befallen him, into which he has fallen, and by which his soul too is ensnared, through what has befallen him.

“Your light has turned to darkness” (Job 22:11). You were in the light when you had your possessions, when your children were alive, when your body was healthy. But now you have gone down, as it were, into darkness, into these straits.
On the same words: That is, in a desolate place, under the open sky, a wanderer, an exile, without a hearth.

“And while you slept, water covered you” (Job 22:11). The words “while you slept, water covered you” mean this: the opposing power covered you, since you were not awake, since you did not sleep. Scripture knows of a certain sleep of sin. That is why it gives us this command: “Do not give sleep to your eyes, nor slumber to your eyelids, so that you may live like a gazelle out of the nooses and like a bird out of the snare” (Proverbs 6:4-5).

“Does not he who dwells on high look upon all?” (Job 22:12). But you think that God, who dwells on high, does not see what is done. As one who looks upon all things, then, he brings down those whose minds are puffed up by a habit of insolence. “And those carried along by insolence he has brought low” (Job 22:12). If anyone is carried along by insolence and, as it were, swept away by a habit and practice of insolence, he is brought low by God. It is likely, then, that since you too treated widows and orphans with insolence and took pledges from your brothers for nothing, this is why you have suffered these things and been brought low.

“And you said: What has the Mighty One known?” (Job 22:13). It is likely that you said to yourself: What has the Mighty One known? As if to say: Can God have known everything? “Or will he judge through the thick darkness?” (Job 22:13).
From the same: God is able to judge even when he is in a storm.
“And he goes about the circle of heaven” (Job 22:14). The providence of God goes the whole way round.

“Will you keep watch on the everlasting path?” (Job 22:15). Can you really keep watch on the everlasting path along which the providence of God travels? “Which righteous men have trodden” (Job 22:15).

From the same: Righteous men have trodden the everlasting path. For they walk along an everlasting path, since everything lies before them to do so that they may attain the age to come. So even if they seem to walk just as others do, their soul itself still sets foot on everlasting paths.

“Who were seized before their time” (Job 22:16). The righteous have often died before their time. For the righteous man, made perfect in a short while, fulfilled long years; for his soul is virtue in the Lord. “Their foundations are an overflowing river” (Job 22:16).
From the same: The foundations of the righteous are of that kind. They are always making progress, always growing in good things.
“And who filled their houses with good things” (Job 22:18).

From the same: He filled the houses of the righteous with good things. I do not take this to mean these houses of ours; rather he filled their houses, those of the ruling part of the soul, with good things. What good things? Self-control, justice, courage, prudence, those that come from the …
